abstract: Abstract Heat stress can significantly affect the survival, metabolism, and reproduction of honeybees. It is important to understand the proteomic changes of honeybees under heat stress to understand the molecular mechanism behind heat resistance. However, the proteomic changes of honeybees under heat stress are poorly understood. We analyzed the proteomic changes of Apis mellifera Ligustica (Hymenoptera: Apidae) under heat stress using mass spectrometry-based proteomics with TMT (Tandem mass tags) stable isotope labeling. A total of 3,799 proteins were identified, 85 of which differentially abundance between experimental groups. The most significant categories affected by heat stress were associated with transcription and translation processes, metabolism, and stress-resistant pathways. We found that heat stress altered the protein profiles in A. mellifera , with momentous resist proteins being upregulated in heat groups. These results show a proof of molecular details that A. mellifera can respond to heat stress by increasing resist proteins. Our findings add research basis for studying the molecular mechanisms of honeybees’ resistance to heat stress. The differentially expressed proteins identified in this study can be used as biomarkers of heat stress in bees, and provide a foundation for future research on honeybees under heat stress. Our in-depth proteomic analysis provides new insights into how bees cope with heat stress.

Materials and Methods
Bees
We selected 3 healthy colonies to obtain frames of sealed brood as colony-level replication from the experimental apiary of Shanxi Agricultural University (Taigu, China). The brood was placed in an incubator at 34 ± 0.5 °C and 75%~80% relative humidity (RH) (
Ma et al. 2019
). After emergence from the cell, the bees were marked on the back with nontoxic, odorless paint, the marked bees were maintained in the colony for further development, and then sampled at the age of 20 days, the marked bees were collected with insect traps at the entrance of the hive (
Li et al. 2019
).
Temperature Stress
Three hundred adults (
n
= 100/hive) were collected and each bee was placed into 15 ml centrifuge tubes with small pores (
Li et al. 2022b
). Bees were then divided into 2 groups (
n
= 50/group/hive) and treated for 2 h at 25 °C, 30% RH and 45 °C, 30% RH, respectively (
Ma et al. 2019
). We randomly picked 10 bees as a colony-level replicate, 3 replicates for each treatment. These samples were frozen in liquid nitrogen and stored at −80 °C for RNA and protein extraction (
Li et al. 2022a
).
Protein Extraction, Protein Digestion, and iTRAQ Labeling
Five entire bees were pooled of each replicate. A total of 3 replicates in each experimental group were analyzed by proteomics. The pooled samples of each replicate were mixed with 2 ml lysis buffer (8 M urea, 2 M thiourea, 4% sodium dodecyl sulfate, 40 mM Tris–HCl, pH = 8.5, 1% phenylmethylsulfonyl fluoride [PMSF]) and sonicated for 30 min and then centrifuged at 20,000×
g
for 10 min at 4 °C (
Qi et al. 2015
). Finally, the protein concentration was measured by Bradford method. We took 500 ug of protein from each sample, reduced it with 30 mM dithiothreitol (DTT) for 60 min at 30° C, and alkylated with 50 mM iodoacetamide in the dark for 45 min at room temperature. Proteins were precipitated with acetone and rinsed (
Zhang et al. 2012
). The sample was dissolved in triethylamine borane (TEAB) buffer and then trypsin-digested at 37 °C for 12 h. The eluted peptide (100 ug/sample) was labeled. iTRAQ reagents 126,128, and 130 were used to label the peptides from control replicates, and iTRAQ reagents 127, 129, and 131 were used to label the peptides from heat stressed replicate.
LC–MS/MS Analysis
Loaded the previously labeled peptide on the C18 column and performed reverse phase separation under alkaline conditions by high performance liquid chromatography (Shimadzu, LC20AD, Waters XBridge Shield C18 RP column, 3.5 µm, 4.6 × 250 mm; Solution A: 100% H
2
O, 5 mM NH
4
OH; Solution B: 80% ACN, 5 mM NH
4
OH; Column temperature 40 °C; Flow rate: 1 ml/min; Phase program: 0–5 min, 5%B; 5–80 min, 5–80%B; 80–82 min, 80–5%B; 82–90 min, 5%B) (
Jiang et al. 2021
). Analyzed each component using the LC–MS/MS (Thermo Acclaim PepMap RSLC, C18 column, 2 µm, 75 µm × 500 mm; Mobile phase buffer A: 100% H
2
O, 0.1% formic acid [FA]; Mobile phase buffer B: 80% acetonitrile [ACN], 0.1% FA; Column temperature 40 °C; Flow rate: 250 nl/min; Phase program: 0–6 min, 2–10%B; 6–51 min, 10–20%B; 51–58 min, 20–80%B; 58–62 min, 80%B; 62–63 min, 80–2%B; 63–70 min, 2%B (
Li et al. 2020
). The electrospray voltage was 2.0 kV and MS scan spectra ranged from 375 to 1,400 m/z and was acquired in the Orbitrap with a resolution of 120,000 and MS2 scan spectrum resolution was 30,000 (
Hu et al. 2016
).
Protein Identification and Quantification
MaxQuant (v.1.5.2.8) was used for iTRAQ protein identification and quantification. For protein identification, the search database was used
A. mellifera
protein database (downloaded from NCBI Feb 2015) and the restriction enzyme digestion method was set to Trypsin/P. For protein quantification, the standard of false discovery rate was set to be less than 0.01.
Bioinformatic Analysis
Gene Ontology (GO) annotations on proteomics were derived from the UniProt-GOA database (
http://www.ebi.ac.uk/GOA/
). We used the Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) pathway database to annotated protein pathways: first, used the KEGG online service tool KAAS to annotated the submitted protein and then used the KEGG mapper to match the annotated protein into the corresponding pathway in the database (
Jiang et al. 2021
).
RNA Extraction, cDNA Synthesis, and Quantitative Real-Time PCR
Total RNA was extracted from the entire bees using TRIzol Reagent (Ambion, Foster City, CA, USA) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. First-strand cDNA was synthesized from 1 μg of total RNA using the ReverTra Ace-a First-Strand cDNA Synthesis Kit (TaKaRa, Shiga, Japan) (
Li et al. 2022b
). Primers for RT-qPCR were designed using Primer 3 software. Primers designed for each gene are provided in
Table 1
. The qRT-PCR thermal cycle procedure was as follows: 95 °C for 30 s; followed by 45 cycles of 95 °C for 5 s and 60 °C for 30 s (
Li et al. 2022a
). All samples were tested in triplicate. The relative quantification of PCR results was conducted using the 2
−∆∆CT
method. The β-actin gene was used as an internal standard.

For qPCR analysis, the mean and SD were calculated from 3 replicates of each experimental group, and the difference analysis was by independent sample

Introduction
Temperature can significantly affect the metabolism and survival of honeybees. In different ecological environments, temperature changes caused by seasonal cycles and other factors have an important impact on the life history of honeybees (
Dalmon et al. 2019
,
Giannoni et al. 2021
). The heat tolerance of honeybees is extremely important to cope with extreme temperatures (
Abou-Shaara et al. 2012
,
Li et al. 2019
). Heat stress can have a significant impact on the survival, reproduction, and metabolism of honeybees, such as causing stress response honeybees, changing the metabolism of honeybees, affecting the survival of adults, and the development of larvae (
Chuda-Mickiewicz and Samborski 2015
,
Alqarni et al. 2019
,
Medina et al. 2020
).
Global warming and an increase in extreme weather and the widespread use of greenhouse pollination, are increasing the risk of heat stress for bees (
Blayt-Erekien et al. 2010
). Honeybees have evolved a number of different adaptive regulatory mechanisms to cope with extreme temperatures. These mechanisms improve the heat tolerance of honeybees, allowing bees to adapt to extreme environmental changes (
Elekonich 2009
,
Shih et al. 2021
). For example, the activity of antioxidant enzymes in honeybees increases under heat stress, which helps to remove oxygen free radicals generated by oxidative stress and prevent cell damage (
Li et al. 2019
); Bees can regulate metabolism through the secretion of neuropeptides from the endocrine system and nervous system, cope with heat stress (
Even et al. 2012
). The most significant response in the molecular level is the induction of heat shock proteins, which can maintain the stability of the cytoskeleton, inhibit protein denaturation, restore the original spatial structure and biological activity of the denatured protein, and effectively improve tolerance (
Collier and Benesch 2020
).
Current knowledge of honeybees heat tolerance physiology does not fully explain the molecular mechanism of honeybees heat tolerance, which calls for new methods to study honeybees heat tolerance (
Ma et al. 2019
). The completion of genome sequencing of
Apis mellifera
has greatly promoted the research on the molecular mechanism of honeybees heat resistance (
Weinstock et al. 2006
).
However, mRNA abundance profiles do not always correlate with protein abundance profiles (
Nagalakshmi et al. 2008
,
de Godoy et al. 2008
, Fu X et al. 2009
). In contrast, proteomics directly measures the biomolecules responsible for the response (
de Hoog and Mann 2004
). Therefore, it is the good way to explore the potential mechanism of adaptation. Since then, researchers have used proteomics to study the stress resistance of honeybees, Nosema–honeybees interactions (
Kurze et al. 2016
), 24-Methylenecholesterol’s effect on honeybees physiology
(Chakrabarti et al. 2020
) and detoxification mechanisms of
A. mellifera
for dietary nicotine (
Rand et al. 2015
).
Honeybees are an important economic insect, it is meaningful to study the proteomics changes of honeybees respond to heat. Studies on the effects of honeybees exposed to high temperature through proteomics can provide important evidence for the physiological effects of high temperature on honeybees.
Apis mellifera
is the most well studied and most widely reared honeybee species, therefore, we use proteomics to study the adaptive mechanisms of
A. mellifera
to high temperature. Those findings may help to improve our understanding of the biological process and mechanism of honeybees heat resistance.

Results
Protein Identification Information
A total of 29,419 peptides were identified through spectral analysis, of which 25,767 were unique peptides. We have identified 3,917 proteins in the normal temperature group and in the high temperature group, 3,799 proteins can be identified (
Supplementary File 1
). A total of 85 proteins displayed significant differential abundance levels after heat stress. Among them, 53 proteins were upregulated, 32 proteins were downregulated (
Fig. 1
;
Supplementary File 2
).
Fig. 1.
Distribution of heat-stress-responsive differentially expressed proteins. The red dots indicate significantly different abundance levels of upregulated proteins, blue dots indicate significant differential abundance of downregulated proteins.
Functional Classification of Differentially Expressed Proteins
To fully understand the proteins identified and quantified in the data, we made a detailed annotation on the functions and characteristics of these proteins, including GO, KEGG pathway, and Clusters of Orthologous Groups of proteins (COG) functional classification (
Supplementary File 3
).
According to molecular function, biological process, and cell composition, GO analysis we used. All differentially expressed proteins were classified into 3 categories, 21 GO terms. The biological process annotation showed that these differentially expressed proteins were primarily involved in cellular process, metabolic processes, biological regulation. Other biological process groups identified were developmental, response to stimulus, reproduction, and immune system, etc. The cellular component annotation showed that these differentially expressed proteins were involved in intracellular, cell, protein-containing complex. The molecular function annotation revealed that the differentially expressed proteins were mainly distributed in binding, catalytic activity. Other groups include transcription regulator activity, structural molecule activity, molecular function regulator (
Fig. 2
;
Supplementary File 4
).
Fig. 2.
Functional category of differentially expressed proteins based on the GO.
Through database comparison and analysis, we performed COG/KOG functional classification statistics for differentially expressed proteins, and the results showed these differentially expressed proteins were classified into 20 COG categories. These categories mainly include lipid transport and metabolism, translation, ribosomal structure and biogenesis, secondary metabolites biosynthesis, transport and catabolism, signal transduction mechanisms (
Fig. 3
;
Supplementary File 5
).
Fig. 3.
Functional category of differentially expressed proteins based on the COG/KOG.
Functional Enrichment Analysis of Differentially Expressed Proteins
We conducted GO and KEGG pathway enrichment analysis for differentially expressed proteins in each comparison group, aiming to understand the enrichment functional types of these differentially expressed proteins.
The enrichment analysis results of 3 types of differentially expressed proteins in GO are shown in
Fig. 4
. Among them, those enriched in biological process mainly include cellular macromolecule biosynthetic process, cell part morphogenesis, cell projection morphogenesis, cell morphogenesis involved in differentiation. Enriched into cellular component mainly include extracellular space, ribonucleoprotein complex, nonmembrane-bounded organelle, intracellular nonmembrane-bounded organelle. Enriched into molecular function mainly include transcription regulator activity (
Supplementary File 6
).
Fig. 4.
GO enrichment of DEPs. A) Biological process and; B) cell composition; C) molecular function. The size of the dots represents the number of differential proteins enriched in the specific GO term. The color of the dots represents the significance of enrichment (
P
value).
The KEGG pathway obtained by enrichment analysis mainly includes peroxisome (
Fig. 5
;
Supplementary File 7
).
Fig. 5.
KEGG enrichment of DEPs. The size of the dots represents the number of differential proteins enriched in the specific KEGG pathway. The color of the dots represents the significance of enrichment (
P
value).
Clustering Analysis
After GO, KEGG pathway of differentially expressed proteins in different groups, we conducted cluster analysis to find the functional correlation of differentially expressed proteins in the comparison groups (
Supplementary File 8
).
For the differentially expressed proteins, we first divided them into 4 groups according to their differential expression multiples, that is Q1–Q4, as shown in the
Supplementary File 9
. Then, we enriched GO and KEGG for each Q group, and conducted cluster analysis to find the functional correlation of proteins with different differentially expressed multiples.
In biological process category, the upregulated proteins were mainly related to negative regulation of metabolic process, ncRNA processing, RNA processing, etc., while downregulated proteins were related to mitotic cell cycle process, glycoprotein biosynthetic process, carbohydrate derivative biosynthetic process, etc (
Fig. 6A
). For cellular component category, the upregulated proteins were mainly related to dynein complex, microtubule associated complex, etc., while downregulated proteins were related to extracellular space, endoplasmic reticulum membrane, endoplasmic reticulum subcompartment, etc. (
Fig. 6B
). In molecular function category, the upregulated proteins were mainly related to transcription regulator activity, protein binding, transcription factor binding, etc, while downregulated proteins were related to transferase activity, transferase activity, transferring acyl groups, cytoskeletal protein binding, etc (
Fig. 6C
).
Fig. 6.
Cluster analysis of DEPs enriched by GO. A) Biological process and; B) cell composition; C) molecular function. Q1–Q4 further divides differential proteins according to multiple changes (Q1 and Q2 are downregulated parts, Q3 and Q4 are upregulated parts; Are the difference scores <0.769, 0.769–0.833, 1.2–1.3, >1.3).
Finally, for the KEGG pathway, the upregulated proteins were mainly related to pancreatic secretion, basal transcription factors, while down regulated proteins were related to longevity regulating pathway—worm and peroxisome (
Fig. 7
;
Supplementary File 10
).
Fig. 7.
Cluster analysis of DEPs enriched by KEGG pathway. Q1–Q4 further divides differential proteins according to multiple changes (Q1 and Q2 are downregulated parts, Q3 and Q4 are upregulated parts; Are the difference scores <0.769, 0.769–0.833, 1.2–1.3, >1.3).
Verification of Differentially Expressed Proteins at the Level of mRNA
In order to examine the trend of corresponding genes encoding differentially expressed proteins protein abundance, we selected 3 key proteins genes (HSP83, CYP450, PLA2) for qRT-PCR analysis. Previous studies have shown that the genes encoding these proteins were heat stress-responsive genes and are important for bees to cope with heat stress (
Ma et al. 2019
). The mRNA abundance trend shows that these 3 genes were consistent with their protein abundance (
Fig. 8
).
Fig. 8.
Comparison of abundance pattern at the mRNA and protein level of DEPs. A) mRNA; B) protein. The color bars represent the relative abundance values of mRNA and protein in different treatment. **The difference between different treatment is extremely significant (
P
< 0.01). The gray columns represent relative expression level in control and black columns represent relative expression level in heat.
Discussion
Heat stress may have an important impact on various physiological and metabolic activities of bees. Here, we used iTRAQ, LC–MS/MS to analyze the protein abundance profile of
A. mellifera
under heat stress, and expansion of the differentially expressed proteins and associated metabolic pathways related to the stress resistance and metabolic changes of bees under heat stress. A total of 3,799 proteins were identified in this study, of which 85 DEPs were identified in the 2 treatment groups (
Supplementary File 2
). The different functions of these DEFs reflect the changes in metabolism and resistance of
A. mellifera
under heat stress. Although due to the technical limitations of iTRAQ, these results cannot fully show the full profile of protein patterns in
A. mellifera
under heat stress, but these results can provide useful information about the adaptability of honeybees to heat stress.
The abundance level of protein is generally related to its mRNA abundance level and post-transcriptional regulatory mechanism (
Buccitelli and Selbach 2020
). In this study, the qRT-PCR results of the 3 validated genes were basically consistent with the results of proteomic analysis, but there were still some differences. The mRNA and protein levels of the 3 validated genes in the high-temperature group were higher than those in the control group, but there were differences in specific differentially expressed multiples and significance of differences. Take into account gene abundance is divided into transcription level and translation level. Protein translation, post-translational modification, and degradation may affect protein levels, which may cause differences in the 2 abundance levels.
According to GO analysis, biological processes of DEPs enrichment mainly include cellular macromolecule biosynthetic process, cell part morphogenesis, cell projection morphogenesis, cell morphogenesis involved in differentiation. This suggests that the metabolic pathways of bees are activated under high temperature stress to cope with stress. On the other hand, it also confirmed that extreme heat can damage honeybee cell structure. Proteins identified were involved in the following cellular component and molecular function: extracellular space, ribonucleoprotein complex, nonmembrane-bounded organelle, intracellular nonmembrane-bounded organelle, transcription regulator activity. These results demonstrate that high temperature stress can enhance cell metabolism and prepare for the production of a range of resistant substances. The peroxisome pathway is the main KEGG pathway obtained by enrichment analysis. This indicates that high temperature stress is one of the factors causing oxidative stress of bees, which confirms our previous conclusions from the perspective of proteomics (
Li et al. 2019
).
We searched for functional correlation of DEPs based on cluster analysis. In biological process category, the upregulated proteins were mainly related to negative regulation of metabolic process, while downregulated proteins were related to mitotic cell cycle process, material synthesis. These evidences indicate that heat stress inhibits the normal physiological metabolism of bees, which is not conducive to their survival. For cellular component and molecular function, the DEPs were mainly related to cell metabolism. In KEGG pathway, the DEPs were mainly related to transcription factors and peroxisome. The results were consistent with those of enrichment analysis.
DEPs of Heat Stress Resistant
Heat stress seriously affects the physiological metabolism of bees. High temperature stress can induce a series of stress responses in bees (
Bordier et al. 2017
). Previous studies have shown that the most important physiological response of bees to stress is the synthesis of heat shock proteins, which can be induced by extreme temperatures, oxidative stress, and toxic substances (
Koo et al. 2015
,
Alqarni et al. 2019
). As a protective protein, it maintains the balance of intracellular proteins, and significantly improves insect tolerance (
Collier and Benesch 2020
). We found 2 proteins related to heat shock proteins, namely Hsp83 and Hsp90 chaperone protein kinase, were expressed differently between 2 groups (
Supplementary File 1
). This result is basically consistent with our previous transcriptome results (
Ma et al. 2019
). The proteome results of other insects under heat stress also confirmed our experimental results. The proteome results of
Drosophila melanogaster
under heat stress showed that multiple heat shock proteins were differentially expressed (
Colinet et al. 2013
). At the translation level, heat shock protein is an important physiological response to heat stress in insects. Heat stress can induce the high expression of several heat shock protein family genes, among which the HSP90 family expression is the most significantly increased. No other heat-shock proteome group was detected in the proteome results. The reason may be that, the time and site of transcription and translation of eukaryotic gene expression exist spatial and temporal gaps, and the starting points of transcription and translation are different. Secondly, after transcription, there will be post-transcriptional processing, degradation of transcription products, translation, post-translational processing, and modification of several levels. So the transcription level and the translation level are not exactly the same; again, because of the different time points tested, the mRNA may have been degraded by the time the protein reached its peak or the amount of protein was still increasing by the time the mRNA reached its peak. Because honeybee exhibits daily rhythms in mRNA and protein level of many genes, driven by circadian clocks (
Rodriguez-Zas et al. 2012
). Finally, differences between individual samples may also contribute to this result. The 2 omics results showed that heat shock proteins play an important role in the resistance to heat stress in
A. mellifera
, especially in the HSP90 family. In addition to the most important heat shock proteins, studies have found that zinc finger proteins (ZFPs) and serine/threonine protein kinases (STKs) are also involved in the organism’s resistance mechanisms to various stresses. ZFPs can regulate gene abundance at the transcriptional level (
Droll et al. 2013
,
Xu et al. 2017
), while protein kinases can regulate protein function (
Krupa et al. 2004
,
Ma et al. 2022
). Various DEPs related to ZFPs and STKs were also found in our results (
Supplementary File 2
). These results were consistent with our previous study on the transcriptome of
A. mellifera
under heat stress, and we also found multiple differentially abundance HSPs and ZFPs (
Ma et al. 2019
). This proves that ZFPs and STKs also play an important role in the metabolic regulation of bees in response to heat stress.
Heat stress will lead to the production of reactive oxygen species (ROS), which cause oxidative damage to the cells (
Slimen et al. 2014
). The increase of oxidative stress will affect the metabolism of bees. However, in the long-term evolutionary process, bees have evolved their own detoxification system. First, endogenous toxin or cytotoxins are metabolized by endogenous enzymes, such as cytochrome P450 (
Haas and Nauen 2021
). Secondly, carboxylesterase is an important detoxification enzyme in insects, and it plays an important role in the detoxification and metabolism of exogenous toxin (
Feng et al. 2018
). Two CYP family members (A0A0K9RP46 and A0A0K9RFX0) and one carboxylesterase (A0A369ANY6) are highly abundance (
Supplementary File 2
). This was also confirmed by our previous studies on the physiological changes of bees under heat stress, which induced an increase in the activities of antioxidant enzymes and detoxifying enzymes in bees (
Li et al. 2019
). The proteomic results of
Bactrocera dorsalis
under heat stress also revealed the differential expression of many REDOX enzymes (
Wei et al. 2015
). These results suggest that heat stress may lead to an increase in ROS, which can harm bees. Detoxification enzymes and antioxidant enzymes may play an important role in removing toxic substances such as ROS caused by high temperature stress.
In addition, we also found that the abundance of PLA2 and interferon increased (
Supplementary File 2
). PLA2 is an important marker for organisms suffering from pressure stress. PLA2 can have an important impact on cell membrane fluidity, membrane protein activity, and other cellular physiological functions (
Gibbons et al. 2013
). Many reports indicate that heat stimulation can cause a large amount of extracellular Ca
2+
to flow into the cell, and the intracellular Ca
2+
concentration is a key factor in the activation of heat shock gene transcription (
Mahalka et al. 2011
). This indicates that heat stress may activate PLA2, which leads to changes in cell membrane fluidity, which in turn increases the intracellular Ca
2+
concentration and activates the abundance of heat shock proteins. PLA2 is an important link in heat shock protein metabolism pathway. Interferon can enhance the phagocytosis and destruction ability of macrophages of immune organs, so as to achieve the functions of regulating immune homeostasis and reducing stress response (
McMenamin et al. 2020
). The increased abundance of interferon indicates that it is involved in the antiheat stress of bees and helps bees reduce the stress response.
DEPs Involved in Transcription and Translation Processes
Bees need to constantly adjust their own metabolism to adapt under high-temperature stress. Regulating transcription and translation is an important regulatory mechanism (
Liu et al. 2020
). In our results, we observed that 8 DEPs related to transcription and translation, such as the 40S and 60S subunits that constitute ribosomes, were upregulated (
Supplementary File 6
). The abundance of RNA polymerase involved in RNA synthesis was downregulated, while the abundance of nuclease was upregulated, all of which can affect gene abundance. Second, there were multiple transcriptional regulators and transcription initiation factors that upregulate abundance. The differential abundance of these proteins may indicate that the body maintains a strong metabolic regulation to respond to environmental changes under high temperature stress.
DEPs Related to Metabolism
Under high temperature stress, the energy metabolism of bees will also change. We found that 2 enzyme proteins related to fatty acid synthesis, Enoyl-(Acyl carrier protein) reductase and Acyl-CoA reductase, were downregulated, which may be due to increased energy requirements of bees in response to stress, inhibits the synthesis of fatty acids and increased energy supply in response to stress (
Chen and Gänzle 2016
). In addition, we also found a number of DEPs related to sugar and amino acid metabolism, including Glycosyl transferase, Protein tyrosine kinase, and Alanine-glyoxylate aminotransferase (
Supplementary File 6
). Glycosyltransferase catalyzes the connection of glycosyl groups to different receptor molecules and participates in a variety of metabolic processes; tyrosine kinases are closely related to cell signal transduction; the high abundance of aminotransferases may be related to the participation in stress-resistant protein synthesis. These results show from one aspect that after bees are subjected to high temperature stress, multiple stress mechanisms in the body are activated to help resist high temperature stress.
We analyzed the changes in protein abundance in
A. mellifera
under high temperature and identified 85 DEPs. The metabolism of
A. mellifera
in the body is vigorous in high temperature environment, and adjusts metabolism to adapt to changes in the environment. Such homeostasis may be mainly attributed to the accumulation of heat shock proteins and detoxification enzymes. The results of this study will help to explore the mechanism of bees’ resistance to heat stress. Our analysis enhances the understanding of the molecular mechanisms of bees’ resistance to heat.
